summary: Looks at data flows in low-power and lossy networks that use RPL for routing, and lists the cases that require the RPL Packet Information option, the source routing header, and IPv6-in-IPv6 encapsulation. It aims to clarify when each is needed in the data plane.

eli5.summary: In networks of tiny sensors, packets sometimes need extra labels or wrapping. This explains exactly when and why.

questions: when is rpl rpi option required
what is the rpl rpi option
when is ipv6 in ipv6 encapsulation needed in rpl
what is rpl storing mode versus non-storing mode
subtitle: When RPL packets need the RPI option, a source routing header, or IPv6-in-IPv6 wrapping, and a new RPI option type.

tldr.problem: Implementers of RPL, the routing protocol for low-power and lossy networks, disagreed about when its data-plane headers are needed or can be omitted. The old RPI option type also made routers drop packets that left the RPL domain.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC works through 24 data-plane use cases for Storing and Non-Storing mode and says for each whether the RPI, the RH3 source route header and IPv6-in-IPv6 encapsulation are needed. It also changes the RPI Option Type from 0x63 to 0x23 and adds a DODAG Configuration option flag so networks can move over without a flag day.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9008 updates RFC 6550, RFC 6553 and RFC 8138. The 0x23 type means packets carrying the RPI can leave the RPL domain without being discarded by RFC 8200 compliant nodes.

today: RFC 9008 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2021, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 6550, RFC 6553 and RFC 8138.

sections.title: Why the RPL Data Plane Needed Clarifying
sections.content:
RPL (RFC 6550) is a routing protocol for constrained networks. Data packets in an RPL network can carry three things the RFC calls RPL artifacts: the RPL Packet Information (RPI), carried in the RPL Option in an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Options header (RFC 6553); the RPL Source Route Header (RH3, RFC 6554); and IPv6-in-IPv6 encapsulation.

Multi-vendor interoperability attempts, and the wish to compress these artifacts, showed that implementers did not agree on when each is necessary. The ROLL working group analyzed how IPv6 rules apply to Storing and Non-Storing RPL and produced 24 data-plane use cases, which the RFC lays out in full. Unconstrained uses of RPL are out of scope.

The RFC also fixes a related problem: it updates RFC 6553 with a new RPI Option Type, so that routers compliant with RFC 8200 ignore the option when they do not recognize it. Encapsulation in most use cases must follow RFC 6040 for the ECN field.
sections.eli5: People building these tiny-sensor networks kept arguing about when a packet needs its special labels. This document settles it case by case.

sections.title: Terms and Node Types
sections.content:
The RFC splits nodes by whether they speak RPL. A RPL leaf is an IPv6 host attached to a RPL router. A RPL-Aware Leaf (RAL) implements RPL. A RPL-Unaware Leaf (RUL) does not, and takes part in the network using Router Advertisements and 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery. A leaf is expected to ignore a consumed Routing Header and a Hop-by-Hop Options header, so it can receive a packet that carries RPL artifacts, but it is not expected to generate them or support IP-in-IP encapsulation.

The 6LoWPAN roles are the 6LoWPAN node (6LN, a leaf here), the 6LoWPAN router (6LR) and the 6LoWPAN border router (6LBR), which is the DODAG root in the reference topology.

The two modes of operation matter a lot. In Storing mode (SM), 6LRs keep routing state for their children so source routing is not needed. In Non-Storing mode (Non-SM), nodes tell the root about their parents, the root knows the topology, 6LRs keep no routing state and downward traffic is source routed. A RPL Instance is either fully Storing or fully Non-Storing.
sections.eli5: Some gadgets in the network know the special RPL rules and some do not. Some towns remember every street (Storing), while in others only the mayor has the map and gives out step-by-step directions (Non-Storing).

sections.title: The New RPI Option Type 0x23
sections.content:
RFC 6553 gave the RPL Option the type 0x63, whose two high bits 01 tell a compliant node to discard the packet if it does not recognize the option. That was chosen to protect the Internet from leaked Hop-by-Hop headers, so packets whose destination was unclear were wrapped in IPv6-in-IPv6. The wrapping costs extra bytes, which means more energy and bandwidth, more chance of loss and possible 6LoWPAN fragmentation.

RFC 9008 changes the type to 0x23: the two high bits become 00, so a node MUST skip over the option and continue, the third bit stays 1 (data may change en route) and the low five bits stay 00011. The relevant clarification is in RFC 8200, where nodes along the path only examine the Hop-by-Hop Options header if configured to do so.

To avoid a flag day, a new DODAG Configuration option flag (bit 3, "RPI 0x23 enable") tells nodes which type the network uses. Flag value 0 keeps the old 0x63, and 1 means 0x23 MUST be used. For Mode of Operation 7, a node MUST use 0x23. Forwarders MUST NOT change the option type, SHOULD use the type they received, and implementations are advised to accept both values. A decompressor of the RFC 8138 RPI-6LoRH MUST use whichever type is active.

The RFC also recommends advertising external targets with Non-Storing mode DAO messaging even in a Storing mode network, so that packets to external targets reach the root and are tunneled to the 6LR that injected the route.
sections.eli5: The old sticker said "throw this away if you do not understand me," so letters leaving the town got trashed. The new sticker says "just ignore me if you do not understand," and a little notice tells everyone which sticker the town is using.

sections.title: Storing Mode Cases
sections.content:
The RFC takes a reference topology of a root (6LBR, node A), 6LRs (B, C, D, E), RALs (F, H, I) and RULs (G, J), and describes each flow with a table of headers added, modified, removed and untouched at each hop. In Storing mode the RPI is always needed, because it helps identify routing loops, while the RH3 is generally not used.

  • Between leaves and the root: RAL to root and root to RAL need no IPv6-in-IPv6. Flows involving a RUL need it: toward a RUL the root encapsulates to the RUL's parent 6LR, and from a RUL the first 6LR encapsulates to the root.
  • Leaf to Internet: a RAL may omit encapsulation and let the RPI reach the Internet, where it is ignored, or may encapsulate to the root. Internet to RAL and Internet to RUL must be encapsulated by the root.
  • Leaf to leaf: RAL to RAL needs no encapsulation; other combinations need it in at least one direction.

For packets leaving toward the Internet, the DODAG root MUST force the Rank in the RPI to zero. An intermediate router that has to add an extension header MUST still encapsulate the packet, because a header can only be removed if it sits in an encapsulating header addressed to that router.
sections.eli5: When a message goes from a gadget that knows the rules to another one nearby, nothing extra is needed. When a gadget that does not know the rules is involved, someone puts the message in an envelope and addresses it to a helper just before the end.

sections.title: Non-Storing Mode Cases
sections.content:
In Non-Storing mode the root knows the whole topology and all traffic flows through it, so only the root needs to compensate for RPL-unaware receivers. The RPI is always expected to be present, because it is needed for routing, quality of service and compression. Downward traffic needs the RH3, and the root must encapsulate it when it is not the originator.

  • Leaf to root: RAL to root and RUL to root use the RPI; a RUL's first 6LR encapsulates the RPI toward the root.
  • Root to leaf: the root adds the RPI and the RH3 itself. Toward a RUL, the RUL ignores both the consumed RH3 and the RPI, so encapsulation is not necessary.
  • Internet to leaf: the root must encapsulate, addressed to the RAL, or to the RUL's parent 6LR, with the RH3 and RPI inside.
  • Between leaves: encapsulation is a must in the downward direction, and in the upward direction it is optional for a RAL source but a must for a RUL source.

The RFC advises setting the IPv6 flow label to zero to help compression, and having the 6LBR set it to a non-zero value when sending toward the Internet.
sections.eli5: In this version the mayor with the map gives the directions, so the mayor can also put the right wrapping on each letter before sending it down the road.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Roughly half the situations involve leaves that do not speak RPL. Some drop packets with RPI or RH3 headers. Per RFC 8200, nodes not configured to examine Hop-by-Hop headers should ignore them, but nodes that predate RFC 8200 or are intolerant will drop such packets, and in general they cannot be easily supported.

They can be supported when the root inserts the artifacts inside an IPv6-in-IPv6 header addressed to the 6LR just before the leaf, since removing the outer header removes the artifacts. That works for Internet-originated traffic in Non-Storing mode, where the root knows the exact topology. Storing mode cannot know the final path, so intolerant leaves cannot be supported there. Traffic originating at the root does not need encapsulation, but can only go to nodes that tolerate the artifacts.

For the move to 0x23, the DODAG root announces it through DIO messages and should change to a new DODAG version. The root stays at 0x63 until it is sure the network can handle 0x23, then switches abruptly. A rebooted node does not remember the type and waits for a DIO that indicates it.
sections.eli5: Some old gadgets throw away anything with unfamiliar stickers. The fix is to wrap the letter so the sticker is removed right before the old gadget.

sections.title: IANA Changes
sections.content: IANA updates the registration of the RPL Option in the Destination Options and Hop-by-Hop Options subregistry from 0x63 to 0x23, and marks 0x63 as deprecated. The "DODAG Configuration Option Flags" subregistry is renamed "DODAG Configuration Option Flags for MOP 0..6", and bit number 3 is registered as "RPI 0x23 enable". Mode of Operation value 7 changes from Unassigned to Reserved, in support of future work.
sections.eli5: The official list of labels is updated: the new sticker number is added, the old one is marked as retired, and one spare slot is kept for later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The considerations of RFC 6553 and RFC 6554 apply inside the RPL domain. The main new worry is the IPv6-in-IPv6 mechanism: each node's willingness to decapsulate and forward packets could be used to disguise the origin of an attack, including a distributed denial of service attack on nodes elsewhere. The RPL root SHOULD either restrict ingress of IPv6-in-IPv6 packets or inspect the header chain, and SHOULD do network ingress filtering (BCP 38) on source addresses in both directions. The RFC recommends against IPsec here, citing the need for a global PKI and tunnel counts that scale with the square of the nodes.

A packet that crosses the border of the RPL domain MAY carry an RH3, and if so that RH3 MUST be fully consumed. The decapsulating node MUST check that an unconsumed RH3 came from inside the RPL domain and drop the packet otherwise. An attacker could also use the RPI to change a packet's priority via a different RPLInstanceID, so the root inserts the RPI inside an encapsulating header on entry. A 6LR acting as border router SHOULD rewrite an RPI that a RUL supplies.
sections.eli5: An extra envelope can hide who a letter really came from. So the town gate checks where letters claim to come from and blocks the suspicious ones.
